# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up is the strongest piece of evidence so far. It answers several open questions directly:
- It adds a second hours measure that doesn't depend on self-report.
- It registers the meetings test before the outcome data existed.
- It runs to 24 months.
- It reports what the meta-analysis's four long studies actually were. They were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, which confirms that "no sign of decay" rested on the designs the meta-analysis itself found inflate effects.

The checkable arithmetic holds:

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Varden per-hour gain, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% |
| Varden per-hour gain, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% |
| Halden continuing organisations, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 | 0.866 (−13.4%) |
| Halden continuing organisations, per-hour gain | 0.968 / 0.866 | +11.8% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% |

The county's staffing estimate also roughly checks out. Treated counter staff worked about 17% fewer hours and were about 6.7% more productive per hour. Restoring staffed capacity therefore needs about 1 / (0.83 × 1.067) ≈ +13% staff, close to the stated 12%. The +9% cost per contact implies labour is about three-quarters of cost, and that assumption should be stated.

There are, however, two problems that change how the decay result should be read, and the mediation claim is stronger than the design supports.

## 1. The Summary overstates the decline by mixing measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is from timesheets and the 8.5% is from system logs. The like-for-like comparison, on timesheets at both points, is 12.5% to 9.8%:
- like-for-like, the decline is 22%;
- the mixed comparison makes it look like 32%.

Section 5's "about a quarter" matches the like-for-like figure, so the Summary and the body disagree.

Separately, the two estimates' CIs overlap almost entirely (+6.9 to +18.4 and +4.6 to +15.2). The paper should report a CI for the change between them before calling it "fading." As it stands, the data are consistent with some decline and also with none.

## 2. Control contamination biases the 24-month estimate toward zero

The "unplanned observation" is presented as a side note, but it bears on the main result. Two of the seven control offices cut meetings at month 15 and gained about 4.1% per hour. Assuming offices of roughly equal size, that alone raises the control mean by about 1.2 percentage points (2/7 × 4.1). The difference-in-differences at 24 months shrinks by about the same amount.

So part of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may be the control group improving, not the treated offices fading. On a rough adjustment, the timesheet gain at 24 months would be around 11%, with a decline of about 1.5 points.

The paper should:
- report the 24-month estimate with and without these two offices;
- compare the two offices against the other five controls over the same period, not only against their own previous six months, which is uncontrolled.

The audit may also have been prompted by staff in those offices learning of the nine-month findings. That would make it spillover from the trial, which should be noted.

## 3. System log time is not the same quantity as timesheet hours

"Active log-in time on the case-management system" records time spent working on cases. It almost certainly excludes meetings, phone calls, training and other non-system work. Timesheets record total working time. This has two consequences.

**The logs-versus-timesheets comparison doesn't show what it claims.** Logs falling 11% against timesheets falling 12% is read as "slightly more work than timesheets." But treated offices cut about 3.5 hours of meetings a week. That alone would shift their remaining time toward case work, so case-system time would fall less than total time even if no unrecorded work existed. The comparison can't distinguish unrecorded work from meeting time turning into case time.

**The mediation needs a mechanism stated.** If meetings are outside the log denominator, cutting meetings doesn't raise output per log-hour by arithmetic. It would have to work through something like less fragmented focus time. That is a plausible mechanism, but it needs to be stated, and it is a different claim from "low-value time removed from the denominator." If instead logs include time when staff are logged in but sitting in a meeting, the paper should say so.

The table also reports log hours as a difference-in-differences, which requires pre-period log data. Logs were "added" at follow-up. Were baseline logs extracted retrospectively from the system? The same question applies to the baseline meeting figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours). The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only at month six.

## 4. The mediation test is not an independent replication

- **Same offices.** Registration at month 11 came before the 24-month outcomes. But the hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices, and mediator data through month 11 had already been seen. This shows the association persisted in the offices that generated it. It does not show it replicates in new ones, and replication was the substance of Varga and Holm's objection. "Survives a registered test" is accurate. Presenting this as a rebuttal of "post hoc" is too strong.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" doesn't add independent information. Treatment was randomised across 14 offices, so the effective sample is 14 clusters. A proportion-mediated estimate of 47% with a CI of 28–66%, built on a total effect whose own CI runs from 3.4% to 13.8%, looks too narrow. Proportion-mediated estimates are unstable when the total effect is modest. Report how the CIs were computed (bootstrap at office level?) and whether a small-cluster correction was applied. That question applies to Table 1 as well.
- **Wording.** The Summary says the test "confirms." The Limitations section correctly says mediation assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome. The Summary should match it, with wording such as "is consistent with" or "supports."

None of this weakens the overall pattern much. Meetings are large and fatigue is smaller, and the uncontrolled two-office observation points the same way. But it is suggestive evidence, not confirmation.

## 5. The Halden subset is not an upper bound

- **The term is wrong.** Selection does bias the estimate upward. But with no comparison group over two years, trends that have nothing to do with the schedule could push the figure in either direction: new software and tools, changes in demand, changes in staff mix. "Upper bound" implies all biases point one way. "Upward-biased by selection and confounded by trend" is accurate.
- **Non-response.** 9 of the 23 organisations didn't provide data. If non-responders were disproportionately ones that reverted or struggled, the 3-of-14 reversion rate is understated.
- **Baseline hours.** The continuing organisations' baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to the 27-organisation figure in the re-analysis. That may be a coincidence, but it is worth checking that it isn't a copied value. It also needs explaining how all 11 have time-tracking data, given that only 17 of the original organisations had both records and time tracking.
- **Framing of the reversions.** The Summary says all three reverted organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." Two cited coverage of opening hours. The third, a marketing agency, is discretionary work by the meta-analysis's own coding, and it cited client deadlines. That is a discretionary organisation finding reduced hours unworkable, and it should be reported as such rather than folded into the coverage story.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Sick days (−27%).** These still aren't normalised by scheduled days. If treated staff work four days, part of the reduction is automatic, as discussed for the nine-month report.
- **Counter waits.** Comparing 7.3 against 4.0 minutes in control offices is an improvement on the nine-month treated-only figure. The control offices' pre-period waits would complete the difference-in-differences.
- **Conflict of interest.** R. Okafor is lead author of the Halden pilot and co-authors a section assessing a critique of it. The Varden authors are likewise assessing a critique of their own hypothesis. Neither is improper, but both should be disclosed.
- **Rebuttal of the re-analysis.** This is fair on substance. The 24-month Varden estimate meets every standard Varga and Holm set (record-based output, actual hours, randomisation, at least 18 months), apart from the question of what the log measure captures (section 3 above). Even on timesheets alone, the gain at 24 months is 9.8% (4.6 to 15.2).

## Bottom line

**Well supported:**
- In discretionary work, a per-hour gain of roughly 8–11% persists at two years under randomised comparison, with output per employee slightly below control.
- Coverage-bound work could not sustain the change without about 12% more staff.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rested on four uncontrolled, scheduled-hours studies.

**Overstated or unresolved:**
- The size of the decline: the Summary mixes measures, and control contamination biases the 24-month estimate toward zero.
- What the log-hours measure captures.
- The mediation result: same offices, 14 clusters, and "confirms."
- The Halden subset as an "upper bound."

**The question that matters most for policy remains open.** Neither the two-office observation nor the trial can say whether cutting meetings without cutting hours would capture most of the gain, because no arm tested it. The obvious next study is a three-arm trial: reduced hours, meeting reorganisation at full hours, and control.

I can draft:
- revised Summary wording;
- a contamination-adjusted sensitivity analysis plan;
- a one-page synthesis of all five documents.
